That is the exact reason why people can still win at a gambling establishment. The house always wins not by consistently beating the individual - that would deter people from returning - but instead by taking a cut of the total turnover from the game. They take this cut by using the house edge - rules that ensure that if someone bets on all the options, they will not break even, but lose a little (usually about 5%).

A simple example is a game of chance:  
A player comes in and bets on a color, winning $10. They then leave the establishment, up $10. The house is now down $10.  
Another player then comes in and bets on the same color, but loses their $10. For the house, this merely brings the loss back down to $0. Every now and then, however, the outcome results in a loss for both color bets. This only has a small chance of happening, so over time the house collects approximately 5% of the total money that comes through the table.

The important part, however, is that nothing beyond what the first player did has any effect on their winnings - which is still $10. So while the gambling establishment is making money (the house always wins), there are still individuals who have also won money during their visit.

And that is the ultimate draw of the gambling establishment - to try your luck at being the one who won.

I think it's misleading to say that the house is always 'winning'. It is making money, but that is not the same thing as winning; just because the house made money does not mean that everyone who visited the gambling establishment on that day lost.  
  
Also, why do you think that nobody bets on "00"? Do you think that there is some disadvantage to betting on 00, as opposed to say number 17 or 29?
I'm just pointing out that the odds are no worse on the double zero than any other number.

But this isn't modding tools; this is a standalone level creator. It's not the same thing, and many companies have made level creators for their games. It doesn't need to be as in-depth as modding tools, which allow you to change the elements of the game; it just needs to be able to move and place objects and assets that already exist and have pre-defined behaviors.  
  
I'm not saying that it wouldn't be a significant process to make, but it certainly is not something that would be impossible or even just financially unfeasible; plenty of smaller companies have released perfectly serviceable level creators for their games. Any extra cost in development would be offset by savings made by not needing design, art, and creative teams also working on it in full capacity.  
  
Whether it would be worth it or not to the company simply comes down to how well it will sell versus the cost of making it, and I would hazard that the cost of making it would be much lower than that of producing a standalone title. I really quite like this game, but it does have a few aspects that were disappointing compared to its predecessor, which came out just prior to its release.  
  
* First of all, the story is really silly. The previous game had an amazing story, even more so than the original, because of the addition of a creepy subplot that added depth. Everything that happens in that game is pretty plausible if you accept the parameters of the story. In this game, however, we are given a bizarre character with an odd appearance who constantly goes on strange monologues. On top of that, the exchanges between two key characters are possibly the most cringeworthy in the series so far, and the exposition is very ham-fisted. Instead of experiencing the story through notes and events that happen to the player, we are given jarring flashbacks and perspective changes. It felt more like a soap opera than a horror game or movie.  
  
* Secondly, the pacing of the game. It starts off really well - the initial setting is fantastic, and the training facility is pretty good (if a little slow near the end), but then the game takes a bizarre turn pacing-wise. We are moved rapidly from location to location, including a strange expedition into a lab from a previous game, which, while it was a cool glimpse at what a remake would be like, was quite obviously just there for fanservice and created way more questions than it answered. The factory also introduced an infamous, immersion-breaking elevator, which confused many players (with good reason). The final areas of the game, which are supposed to be the most engaging, ended up being a pretty linear series of rooms that just lead to the last boss.   
  
* Thirdly, the new gameplay mechanics. They were actually pretty cool ideas - no more item box backtracking, and some extra gameplay in the form of character switching. Unfortunately, the item design that was supposed to combat backtracking was completely pointless, as it just resulted in designated 'item rooms' anyway, which were usually right next to a save point, just as the original item boxes were. It actually caused more problems, because the game designers no longer had to worry too much about players running out of inventory space, as they could just drop items. So we have lots of items in the game that take up two slots, and end up being ferried around from location to location (looking at you, specific item). Combine that with the constant item juggling between characters, and the ability to make bad decisions when splitting up that can adversely affect your experience (do NOT send one character up stairs in the lab), and the result is a much more frustrating and less immersive experience. 
  
Look, this game is still great. I prefer it to some other entries in the series, but compared to the beautiful pacing and atmosphere of its predecessor and other earlier titles, it simply doesn't hold up as well.

Voice acting is a challenging industry, so for anyone considering it as a career, unions are essential. Unfortunately, there is always a large pool of new and inexperienced talent that these localization companies can exploit.

For a voice actor, royalties are fair pay. The reason for this is the very same as what is happening to a well-known voice actor now; voice actors are easily replaced. They have zero job security, because unlike a regular actor whose face is a key aspect of their character's identity, voice actors can be dismissed the moment they request any kind of pay increase. Of course, the natural result of this is that studios can go the other way - completely underpay voice actors, because they need all the work they can get. View the work history of a standard television actor and you'll see a handful of different shows, but look at the history for the same level voice actor, and you'll often see hundreds of different projects, shows, and games. The voice actor is earning a fraction of what an actor would be. "Voice actors should get properly paid for the work up front and that should be the end of it." is completely true - but the reality is that they don't. Ironically, the only voice actors who get paid adequately are the ones who are already big name actors - and they also often turn out to be poor voice actors. 

I personally dislike the state of most industry unions, but the voice acting union is one of the few that really does need support, because even with it they still face significant challenges.
